pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 12–14 years

- **Topic:** Earth's Atmosphere & CO2

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Chemistry, Earth and atmosphere):** pupils are taught "the composition of the atmosphere" and "the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and the impact on climate," building the link between combustion of fossil fuels, rising atmospheric CO2 and global warming.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-ESS3-5):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-5] — principally human release of greenhouse gases.

- **Operational details:** First fix the composition: today's atmosphere is roughly 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, ~1% argon, and only about 0.04% carbon dioxide plus trace gases and water vapour — so CO2 is tiny yet climatically powerful. Establish CO2 as a greenhouse gas: it lets sunlight in but absorbs and re-radiates outgoing infrared, warming the surface (the natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable; the ENHANCED effect from extra CO2 causes warming). Connect human activity — burning fossil fuels for energy and transport, deforestation — to the measured rise in atmospheric CO2 and to rising global average temperature and its consequences. Emphasise EVIDENCE: the Keeling-curve rise in CO2 and the century-scale temperature record. Keep it qualitative and correlational-with-mechanism at KS3; avoid detailed radiative-forcing maths.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier C (formal, evidence-based). The child states the atmosphere's main composition, explains how CO2 acts as a greenhouse gas, links human fossil-fuel use to rising CO2 and temperature, and cites evidence for the trend.
bestPractices: Fix the composition quantitatively first (78% N2, 21% O2, ~0.04% CO2) so pupils grasp that CO2 is a trace gas with outsized climatic effect.
Teach the greenhouse mechanism as selective: sunlight in, outgoing infrared absorbed and re-radiated — and distinguish the natural (habitable) effect from the enhanced (warming) effect.
Build the causal chain explicitly: burn fossil fuels → CO2 rises → more infrared trapped → global temperature rises, rather than a vague 'pollution causes warming'.
Ground the claim in evidence pupils can read — the rising CO2 (Keeling) curve and the century temperature record — to develop 'how do we know?' reasoning.
Keep it qualitative and mechanism-based at KS3; avoid radiative-forcing calculations and defer detailed climate modelling.
keyRepresentations: A composition pie/bar of the atmosphere (N2, O2, Ar, CO2, trace).
A greenhouse-effect diagram: incoming sunlight, outgoing infrared, CO2 absorbing/re-radiating.
A global-average-temperature time series over the past century.
A causal-chain flow: fossil fuels → CO2 → trapped IR → warming.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking CO2 makes up a large fraction of the air, rather than only ~0.04%.
Confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole, or believing warming comes from a 'hole' letting more sunlight in.
Believing the natural greenhouse effect is bad, missing that it keeps Earth habitable and only the enhanced effect is the problem.
Thinking CO2 blocks incoming sunlight rather than trapping outgoing infrared.
Assuming because CO2 is a tiny percentage it cannot matter for climate.

learn.summary: For 12–14 year olds: establish the atmosphere's composition (~78% nitrogen, ~21% oxygen, ~1% argon, ~0.04% CO2), show that CO2 is a trace gas with an outsized climatic effect, explain the greenhouse mechanism (sunlight in, outgoing infrared absorbed and re-radiated), distinguish the natural (habitable) from the enhanced (warming) greenhouse effect, and connect human fossil-fuel burning and deforestation to rising CO2, rising global temperature, and at least one specific consequence (e.g. rising sea levels, more extreme weather), using evidence (the Keeling CO2 curve and the century-scale temperature record). Keep it qualitative and mechanism-based at KS3; avoid radiative-forcing maths. Several complementary media are offered: a driveable model, a diagram/cross-section scaffold, an evidence-focused dialogue, and a checkpoint, each with a stated affordance and limit.

activities.title: Drive a two-part climate model: greenhouse effect and emissions
feedback: If the learner expects CO2 to block incoming sunlight, point them back to the model: sunlight still comes in; it is the OUTGOING infrared that is absorbed and re-radiated.

If the learner thinks a 0.04% gas cannot matter, have them vary only the CO2 control and note that a small slice still visibly moves the thermometer: separate 'how much there is' from 'how powerful it is'.
If the learner treats all greenhouse warming as bad, use the natural baseline level to show the effect keeps Earth habitable; only the enhanced effect from extra CO2 is the problem.
activities.rationale: Causal systems (radiation balance; emissions → CO2 → temperature) reward acting on variables and observing the response, which may help turn an abstract and politically loaded claim into an observed mechanism. The composition pie and a Keeling-shaped curve tie the model to the quantitative facts and real evidence pupils should reason about.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught the composition of the atmosphere and the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and its impact on climate.
Dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, ~1% argon and ~0.04% carbon dioxide.
learnerActions: Start from the greenhouse view: watch sunlight stream onto the surface and infrared radiate back out toward space.

Move a CO2 control to thicken the atmospheric 'blanket' so more outgoing infrared is re-radiated back down, and read the thermometer as it changes; compare the natural baseline level with an enhanced (higher-CO2) level.
Read a composition pie showing CO2 as roughly 0.04% of the air, then state in your own words how such a small slice can still change the temperature you just observed.
Switch to the emissions view and raise the fossil-fuel-burning and deforestation controls; watch the atmospheric-CO2 graph rise (echoing the real Keeling curve) and a global-temperature trace follow.
Write the causal chain the model produced: burn fossil fuels / deforest → CO2 rises → more infrared trapped → global temperature rises.
activities.intendedInsight: CO2 is a trace gas (~0.04%) yet climatically powerful because it absorbs and re-emits outgoing infrared; human emissions raise CO2, which raises global temperature — a cause-and-effect chain the learner generates rather than a slogan.

activities.title: Explore a labelled atmosphere cross-section and greenhouse diagram
feedback: If a learner names oxygen as the biggest gas, return to the pie: nitrogen is ~78%, oxygen ~21%.
If a learner says CO2 stops sunlight entering, re-reveal the diagram's two arrows: sunlight in, infrared out — CO2 acts on the outgoing infrared.
activities.rationale: A tappable cross-section and labelled diagram can efficiently establish composition and the radiation geometry and surface human sources. This is a scaffold: a fixed diagram orients learners but does not let them vary CO2 and observe a temperature response, so it should precede or accompany the driveable model rather than replace it.
sourceClaims: Dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, ~1% argon and ~0.04% carbon dioxide.
learnerActions: Examine a layered illustration of the atmosphere with a composition pie (78% N2, 21% O2, ~1% Ar, ~0.04% CO2) and name the main gases in order.
Tap the Sun, the surface, and CO2 molecules on a greenhouse-effect diagram to reveal how incoming sunlight is absorbed and outgoing infrared is trapped and re-radiated.
Identify human sources of CO2 (fossil-fuel burning, deforestation) highlighted on the diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: Orient to atmospheric composition and the in/out radiation idea: nitrogen dominates, CO2 is a trace gas, and the greenhouse mechanism acts on outgoing infrared.

activities.title: Question a climate scientist about the evidence
feedback: If the learner attributes warming to the ozone hole or a hotter Sun, have the scientist distinguish the problems: ozone loss lets more UV through; the greenhouse effect traps outgoing infrared.

If the learner thinks CO2's small abundance means it cannot matter, the scientist should separate how much CO2 there is from how strongly it absorbs infrared, while noting that adding more CO2 does increase the warming effect.

If the learner cannot name a consequence, have the scientist connect higher temperatures to a concrete example, e.g. melting land ice (glaciers and ice sheets) and the expansion of warming seawater raising sea levels, or more frequent extreme-weather events.
activities.rationale: An in-role climate scientist the learner can question supports the evidence-and-argument strand and can address misconceptions through dialogue, including linking warming to a specific consequence. It complements but does not itself deliver the manipulate-and-observe mechanism, so pair it with the model or diagram.
learnerActions: Ask an in-role climate scientist 'how do we know?' questions about rising CO2 and temperature.
Have the scientist explain the Keeling CO2 curve and the century-scale temperature record and where the data come from.
Ask the scientist about one specific consequence of the warming (e.g. rising sea levels or more extreme weather) and how it follows from higher global temperatures.
Answer the scientist's probing questions, e.g. why a 0.04% gas can matter and how the greenhouse effect differs from the ozone hole.
activities.intendedInsight: The human–CO2–warming link rests on readable evidence (rising CO2 curve, temperature record) and leads to concrete consequences such as rising sea levels or more extreme weather; 'how do we know?' reasoning distinguishes mechanism from slogan.

activities.title: Checkpoint: composition, mechanism, causal chain, consequence and graph reading
feedback: For composition errors, restate ~78% N2, ~21% O2, ~1% Ar, ~0.04% CO2 and show the pie.
For a chain mis-ordering, remind that CO2 must rise before more infrared is trapped and before temperature rises.
If a consequence is missing or wrong, link higher global temperature to a concrete outcome such as rising sea levels or more frequent extreme weather.
For graph-reading errors, point to the rising CO2 (Keeling) curve and the century temperature record as the evidence base.
activities.rationale: Composition, greenhouse-gas identification, chain sequencing, naming a consequence and graph reading are directly checkable. Recognition and ordering confirm recall and sequencing but do not elicit the learner-generated manipulation of the model, so use this to assess after the model or diagram work.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils are taught the composition of the atmosphere and the production of carbon dioxide by human activity and its impact on climate.
Dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, ~1% argon and ~0.04% carbon dioxide.
learnerActions: Set or select the approximate percentages of N2, O2, Ar and CO2 (e.g. 78% / 21% / ~1% / ~0.04%).
Choose which gases are greenhouse gases and which are not.
Put the causal chain in order: burn fossil fuels → CO2 rises → more infrared trapped → temperature rises.
Identify one specific consequence of climate change (e.g. rising sea levels, more extreme weather).
Read a CO2/temperature graph and state what the trend shows and why it matters.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidate the facts and the chain: correct composition, which gases trap infrared, the ordered cause-and-effect, a named consequence, and interpretation of trend data.

constraints: Keep the treatment qualitative and mechanism-based at KS3: avoid radiative-forcing calculations and detailed climate modelling (per the pedagogy guidance).
Always distinguish the natural greenhouse effect (keeps Earth habitable) from the enhanced effect (from extra human CO2) so learners do not treat all greenhouse warming as harmful.

Insist the greenhouse mechanism acts on OUTGOING infrared, not on blocking incoming sunlight; and that CO2 matters despite its small abundance because it absorbs infrared (unlike the far more abundant N2 and O2), while still recognising that adding more CO2 strengthens the effect.
Include at least one specific, concrete consequence of warming (e.g. rising sea levels, more extreme weather) so the objective's final evidence item is met.
The labelled diagram/cross-section is an orientation scaffold: a fixed image cannot be varied to show the temperature response, so it supports but does not replace manipulate-and-observe work.
The checkpoint assesses recall, sequencing, naming a consequence and graph reading; recognition/sequencing responses do not elicit the learner's independent construction of the mechanism.
The dialogue with an in-role scientist supports evidence reasoning but does not itself provide the manipulate-and-observe mechanism; pair it with a model or diagram.
A model thermometer/CO2 control is a qualitative illustration of trend and direction, not a quantitative prediction of real climate magnitudes.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The objective's fourth evidence item (discuss one specific consequence of climate change) was absent from the original candidate's activities and has been incorporated into the scientist conversation, the checkpoint and the summary.

The legacy row rated 3D as 'poor' claiming it 'adds cost without conceptual gain'; this comparative-necessity claim is not established by the sources and has been omitted rather than asserted. The 2D linked model is proposed on the stated affordance that radiation in/out, concentration and temperature map cleanly onto 2D views.

The legacy 'possible' ratings implied static reveals 'cannot' carry the mechanism; this was softened to a scoped scaffold limit (a fixed diagram cannot be varied to show a temperature response) rather than a universal claim that static images cannot teach.

The POE candle-and-jar demonstration from the assessment field is deliberately not converted into a learner activity: water rising ~1/5 is an approximate and somewhat unreliable indicator of oxygen fraction (heating/cooling of the trapped gas, CO2 solubility, and extinction from CO2 build-up and reduced oxygen before all oxygen is used all affect the result), so it is left in the assessment field and flagged as uncertain rather than taught as a clean 'water rises ~20% = oxygen fraction' result.
Two source claims used here (NGSS MS-ESS3-5 and the RSC composition figure) carry verified:false in the row; treat associated claims as legacy-unverified.

assess.poeTask: Predict-Observe-Explain: float a candle in a dish of water, light it, and invert a jar over it. Ask the child to predict how much of the jar's air the candle can use before going out — and how far the water will rise — and WHY. A child who thinks air is mostly oxygen predicts the water rises most of the way. The candle goes out after consuming only ~1/5 (the oxygen), water rising ~20%. The pre-observation reasoning about composition is the diagnostic part.
probeDeeper: If CO₂ is only about 0.04% of the air, how can adding a bit more matter so much?
What's the difference between the hole in the ozone layer and the greenhouse effect?
Nitrogen and oxygen don't trap heat but CO₂ does — what's special about the CO₂ molecule?
Would Earth be warmer or colder with NO greenhouse effect at all? So is the effect itself the problem?
assess.correctAnswer: Air is mostly NITROGEN (~78%), then oxygen (~21%); CO₂ is only a tiny fraction (~0.04%). Even so, CO₂ is a greenhouse gas: it absorbs and re-emits the infrared (heat) radiation the Earth gives off, trapping energy in the atmosphere. A small percentage change in a powerful heat-trapping gas has a large warming effect. Full marks correct the composition AND explain warming by the greenhouse (infrared-trapping) mechanism, not by CO₂'s abundance.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Correct the proportions explicitly: ~78% nitrogen, ~21% oxygen, ~1% argon, ~0.04% CO₂. Use a pie chart or a jar-of-beads model.
errorPatterns.distractor: Oxygen is the biggest gas, and CO₂ is a large slice too.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: names oxygen as the main gas; can't state nitrogen is ~78%

errorPatterns.pattern: CO₂ must be a large fraction of air to affect climate ('it warms because there's loads of it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain potency: CO₂ absorbs/re-emits infrared strongly, so a trace still traps a lot of heat. Small % change, large effect. Separate 'how much' from 'how powerful'.
errorPatterns.distractor: It must be a big chunk of the air, or it couldn't warm anything.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: ties CO₂'s effect to abundance rather than its infrared-trapping property

errorPatterns.pattern: global warming is caused by the hole in the ozone layer / by the Sun getting hotter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish the two problems: ozone loss lets more UV through; the greenhouse effect traps outgoing infrared. Climate warming is the greenhouse mechanism, driven by emissions.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's really the hole in the ozone layer letting more heat in.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: attributes warming to ozone depletion or a hotter Sun rather than trapped infrared

errorPatterns.pattern: the greenhouse effect is entirely bad / man-made from scratch (no natural greenhouse effect)
errorPatterns.nextMove: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough to live on; the PROBLEM is the ENHANCED effect from extra human CO₂. Distinguish natural from enhanced.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: thinks all greenhouse warming is harmful and human-invented; unaware the natural effect makes Earth habitable

responseLevels.gap: Thinks air is mostly oxygen or CO₂ is abundant; attributes warming to the ozone hole or to CO₂'s quantity; conflates natural and enhanced effects.
responseLevels.full: Gives the correct composition (N₂-dominated, trace CO₂), explains warming by CO₂ absorbing/re-emitting infrared, distinguishes the natural from the enhanced greenhouse effect and from ozone depletion, and links human activity (fossil fuels, deforestation) to a specific climate consequence.
responseLevels.partial: States the composition roughly and that CO₂ causes warming, but can't explain the infrared-trapping mechanism or why a trace gas matters, or muddles ozone with the greenhouse effect — facts without the causal chain.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A student says 'the air is mostly oxygen, and carbon dioxide makes up a big chunk of it too — that's why more CO₂ is warming the planet so much.' What's actually the biggest gas in the air, and roughly how much of it is CO₂? Then the important part: if CO₂ is such a tiny fraction, explain how adding more of it can still change the climate.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The tier-two reason separates a child who knows the real composition (N₂-dominated, trace CO₂) and the greenhouse mechanism (CO₂ traps infrared) from one who assumes air is mostly oxygen or that CO₂ warms because there's 'a lot' of it. It also flushes out confusion between the greenhouse effect and the ozone hole.
